reason: The text demonstrates the opposite of this statement. Pharaoh, despite his elite status as king and his great power, is repeatedly humbled before God and his authority is undermined throughout the narrative. The Hebrew slaves—the regular, enslaved people—are shown as God's chosen ones whom He protects and whom He will free. The plagues affect both the elite and common people of Egypt, but only those (both elite and common) who fear God's word and obey it experience protection or benefit. Pharaoh's elite position does not make him inherently better or morally superior; rather, his hardened heart and refusal to listen to God are portrayed as spiritual blindness. The narrative emphasizes that righteousness, obedience, and fear of God—not social status or elite position—determine one's standing.
